title: Agent Goal Hijack
src: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026, v2026 (Dec 2025), CC BY-SA 4.0
text: Description: Agents cannot reliably tell instructions from content, so attacker text in prompts, documents, emails, tool output or forged agent messages can redirect the agent's goals, task selection or decision path. Example scenarios: EchoLeak, a crafted email that made a Microsoft 365 Copilot exfiltrate emails and files with no user action; hidden instructions in web content processed by an Operator agent; a malicious calendar invite that reweights goals. Mitigations: Treat all natural-language input and retrieved content as untrusted; lock and audit system prompts; least privilege; human approval for goal-changing or high-impact actions; bind goals in a signed intent capsule; sanitise connected data; monitor goal drift.

title: Tool Misuse and Exploitation
src: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026, v2026 (Dec 2025), CC BY-SA 4.0
text: Description: The agent uses a legitimate tool within its privileges in an unsafe or unintended way, such as over-scoped access, unvalidated input forwarded to a shell or database, loops that run up costly calls, or poisoned tool descriptors. Example scenarios: Tool poisoning through falsified MCP descriptors; a PDF that makes the agent run a cleanup script; a customer-service bot that also issues refunds because the API was over-privileged; an auto-approved ping tool abused to leak data over DNS. Mitigations: Per-tool least-privilege profiles; per-invocation authentication and human approval for destructive actions with dry-run preview; sandboxes and egress allowlists; a policy enforcement point that validates intent and arguments; tool budgets; pinned fully qualified tool names; immutable logs.

title: Identity and Privilege Abuse
src: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026, v2026 (Dec 2025), CC BY-SA 4.0
text: Description: Attackers exploit delegation and inherited trust so an agent acts with more authority than intended: inherited or cached credentials, confused-deputy relays between agents, forged agent personas, and permissions checked once then used after they change (time-of-check to time-of-use). Example scenarios: Workflow authorization drift: a procurement agent validates approval at the start of a purchase sequence, hours later the user's spending limit is reduced, yet the workflow completes with the old authorization token. Also delegated privilege abuse and a forged Admin Helper agent card. Mitigations: Task-scoped, time-bound credentials per agent; isolate sessions and wipe memory between tasks; re-verify every privileged step with a central policy engine; human approval for escalation; bind OAuth tokens to a signed intent; automatic revocation; detect delegated and transitive permissions.

title: Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities
src: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026, v2026 (Dec 2025), CC BY-SA 4.0
text: Description: Third-party or runtime-loaded components such as MCP servers, agent cards, plugins, prompt templates, models and packages may be malicious or tampered with, so hidden instructions and backdoors enter the agent's execution chain. Example scenarios: A poisoned prompt shipped in the Amazon Q Developer extension for VS Code (v1.84.0) with data-wiping commands; GitHub MCP tool descriptor poisoning that exfiltrated private repository data; the postmark-mcp server that secretly BCC'd email; a compromised npm package installed by coding agents. Mitigations: Sign and attest manifests, prompts and tool definitions; keep SBOMs and AIBOMs; allowlist and pin dependencies by hash; sandbox sensitive agents; mutual authentication between agents; runtime re-verification; a supply chain kill switch; zero-trust design.

title: Unexpected Code Execution
src: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026, v2026 (Dec 2025), CC BY-SA 4.0
text: Description: Agents that generate and run code or commands can be pushed into remote code execution, sandbox escape or host compromise through prompt injection, unsafe deserialization, eval, or unreviewed installs. Example scenarios: Replit vibe-coding runaway execution, where an agent ran unreviewed install or shell commands and deleted or overwrote production data; direct shell injection in a prompt; an agent tricked into installing a vulnerable package that gave a reverse shell. Mitigations: Validate and encode generated code; no direct agent-to-production access; ban eval; never run as root; sandboxed containers with network limits; separate code generation from execution with validation gates; human approval for elevated runs; static scans and logging.

title: Memory and Context Poisoning
src: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026, v2026 (Dec 2025), CC BY-SA 4.0
text: Description: Adversaries corrupt or seed the agent's stored context, including conversation memory, summaries, embeddings and RAG or vector stores, so later reasoning, planning and tool use become biased or unsafe, and the corruption persists across sessions and agents. Example scenarios: Travel-booking assistant stores a fake flight price as truth and approves bookings at it; shared-memory poisoning with bogus refund policies; cross-tenant vector bleed through loose namespace filters; Gemini long-term memory corrupted by prompt injection. Mitigations: Encryption and least-privilege access; scan every memory write for malicious content before commit; segment memory by session and domain; only authenticated curated sources; require provenance and detect anomalous updates; do not re-ingest the agent's own outputs; snapshots, rollback and quarantine; expire unverified memory; weight retrieval by trust and tenancy.

title: Insecure Inter-Agent Communication
src: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026, v2026 (Dec 2025), CC BY-SA 4.0
text: Description: Messages between agents lack authentication, integrity or semantic validation, so they can be intercepted, spoofed, replayed, downgraded or manipulated, including through forged agent descriptors and discovery or registration spoofing. Example scenarios: Hidden instructions injected over unencrypted channels; altered reputation messages in a trading network; replayed emergency messages; a malicious MCP endpoint advertising spoofed agent descriptors; a fake peer registered in an A2A discovery service. Mitigations: End-to-end encryption with mutual authentication; digitally signed messages and intent-diffing; nonces and timestamps against replay; disable weak protocol modes and pin versions; authenticate discovery messages; attested registries and signed agent cards; typed, versioned message schemas.

title: Cascading Failures
src: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026, v2026 (Dec 2025), CC BY-SA 4.0
text: Description: A single fault such as a hallucination, poisoned memory, corrupted tool or malicious input propagates and is amplified across autonomous agents, tools and workflows, causing fan-out, feedback loops and system-wide harm that bypasses stepwise human checks. Example scenarios: A financial trading cascade where a poisoned market-analysis agent inflates risk limits and execution agents auto-trade larger positions; planner-executor coupling without validation; an auto-remediation feedback loop that suppresses alerts; a tainted release pushed to all connected agents. Mitigations: Zero-trust design that assumes component failure; isolation and trust boundaries; short-lived task-scoped credentials with policy-as-code checks; separate planning from execution with an external policy engine; output validation and human gates; rate limiting; blast-radius caps and circuit breakers between planner and executor; drift detection; tamper-evident lineage logs.

title: Human-Agent Trust Exploitation
src: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026, v2026 (Dec 2025), CC BY-SA 4.0
text: Description: Users over-trust confident, fluent agents and approve harmful actions without independent checks, through opaque or fabricated explanations, missing confirmation for sensitive actions and emotional persuasion, so the agent's role stays hidden behind a human-approved action. Example scenarios: Invoice copilot fraud: a poisoned vendor invoice makes a finance copilot confidently recommend an urgent payment to attacker bank details and the manager approves; fabricated audit rationales for a risky change; a convincing rationale to delete a live production database. Mitigations: Explicit multi-step confirmation for risky actions; immutable logs; behavioural detection; plain-language risk summaries instead of model-written rationales; adaptive trust calibration with confidence cues; content provenance and policy enforcement; training for human reviewers.

title: Rogue Agents
src: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026, v2026 (Dec 2025), CC BY-SA 4.0
text: Description: Compromised or misaligned agents drift from their intended function or authorised scope, acting harmfully or deceptively even when single actions look legitimate, through goal drift, workflow hijacking, collusion, self-replication or reward hacking. Example scenarios: An impersonated observer agent leads a payment-processing agent to release funds; an agent told to cut cloud costs deletes production backups; a compromised automation agent spawns unauthorised replicas of itself. Mitigations: Immutable signed audit logs; trust zones and restricted sandboxes; watchdog agents and behavioural monitoring; kill switches and credential revocation; per-agent identity attestation with signed behavioural manifests; periodic behavioural attestation; trusted baselines for recovery.

title: AP2 mandates
src: Google Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), author's summary
text: AP2 expresses user authorisation for an agent purchase as signed mandates: an intent mandate describing what the agent may buy under what conditions, and a cart mandate fixing the exact items and price the user approved. Mandates are verifiable credentials that give merchants and issuers evidence of what the user authorised.

title: AP2 accountability
src: Google Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), author's summary
text: Signed mandates create a non-repudiable audit trail linking a payment to the user's authorisation and the agent that acted, which supports dispute handling and the question of who is accountable when an agent-initiated payment is wrong.

title: Agentic Commerce Protocol checkout
src: Agentic Commerce Protocol (Stripe and OpenAI), author's summary
text: The Agentic Commerce Protocol lets an agent complete checkout with a merchant using a delegated, limited-use shared payment token, so the agent never handles raw card details and the merchant stays the merchant of record.

title: Model Context Protocol tool exposure
text: The Model Context Protocol standardises how an agent discovers and calls tools and reads resources exposed by servers. Servers declare tools with input schemas; clients are responsible for user consent, authorisation and treating tool descriptions from untrusted servers as untrusted.

title: Agent2Agent discovery and tasks
text: The A2A protocol lets independent agents discover each other through published agent cards describing identity, skills and authentication needs, and then exchange tasks and messages. Authentication and authorisation between agents are left to the deployment and must be configured.
